title: CP System
notes: Triaged 7 November 2026: write as hardware/cp-system (non-consumer arcade board, following the Model 2 precedent). Scope: Capcom's standard arcade platform 1988-1995, later CPS-1: design aims, stacked A/B/C boards with game ROMs on their own board, 68000/Z80/YM2151/OKI MSM6295, 384x224 picture and layers, CPS-B protection and the CPS-B-21 suicide battery, games, bootlegs, CP System Dash in outline, the CPS Changer, and emulation history (Callus, MAME). Out of scope: CPS-2/CPS-3 beyond a successor paragraph, QSound (VC-0154), X68000 (VC-0174), JAMMA (VC-0115). Coverage checked: no entry, title, alias or redirect for CP System/CPS-1/CPS1/CPS; survey sections only in hardware/arcade-hardware and companies/capcom; eleven other reviewed entries mention it. Open and closed website issues searched; no prior issue. Disagreements kept visible: development cost (TGM's £5.5 million vs a flyer's five million dollars), ACE's two 68000s (there is one; Italy's K is ACE's licensed edition, not independent), Strider vs Ghouls 'n Ghosts as second game, about thirty games. Source leads: The Games Machine 19 (June 1989); ACE 26 and C+VG 96 (Nov 1989); Edge 7 (1994) and 133 (2004); K (Italy) 12; The Games Machine (Italy) 105 (1998); SuperGamePower (Brazil) March 1995 and February 1999; MAME cps1 driver; Fabien Sanglard's The Book of CP-System (modern study; Gamest #38 and Akiman quotes reach us only through it); Wireframe 54; Retro Gamer 42; gamesTM's Retro: The Ultimate Retro Companion vol. 2 (not a Retro Gamer publication). Gaps: a Japanese period source for the CPS Changer; the Gamest text for the Tsujimoto quote. discontinued left unset: 1995 marks the last new game, not end of production. Draft and claim check done; follow-ups VC-3189 to VC-3193.

title: Magnavox Odyssey
notes: Triaged 7 November 2026: write as systems/magnavox-odyssey (the platform ID existing entries already use). Scope: the 1972 Odyssey (model 1TL200) as a product, from Magnavox's January 1971 preliminary agreement for the Sanders Brown Box and the Skill-O-Vision field tests, through the May 1972 launch, the card-and-overlay design, twelve packed-in games, the rifle and game packs, pricing and sales, export versions (Mexico, Germany/ITT, Brazil/Planil, the twelve-country export model), to the Odyssey 100 and 200 in 1975. Prototype history and patent cases stay in people/ralph-baer and games/pong; Odyssey² is VC-0124; Sanders is VC-1206. Coverage checked: no entry, title, alias or redirect; sections in people/ralph-baer and games/pong, passing mentions in nine other entries. Open and closed website issues searched (VC-0123, Odyssey, Magnavox, Skill-O-Vision, Brown Box, Ralph Baer, 1TL200); none. Dates: introduced 1972, discontinued 1975. Disagreements recorded in prose: 1972 sales (close to 100,000) vs production (140,100 Baer, 130,000+ Winter/Retro Gamer); total 330,000-350,000; launch month May vs August 1972; $79 price cut early vs late 1973; C vs D batteries; Video Games' later 'Odyssey 100' misnaming. Source leads: Ralph Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (2005); Video Games Feb 1983 (Bloom interview) and Jan 1984 (Lovece); Electronic Games March 1982; Retro Gamer Videogames Hardware Handbook vol. 1 (Goldberg); David Winter's PONG-Story (follows Baer closely on marketing, so not independent there); Computer History Museum catalogue 102752091. Gaps: a Brazilian period source for Planil; a period source for the Philips takeover year. Draft and claim check done; follow-ups VC-3194 to VC-3198.

title: VRC6
notes: Triaged 7 November 2026: this combined row is written as its main subject, the VRC6, at hardware/vrc6. The general Famicom expansion-audio survey stays in the reviewed hardware/apu table; the lesser-known chips are split to VC-3204, and VRC7 and Namco 163 to VC-3201 and VC-3202. Scope: two pulse channels with 1/16-step duty and a constant-output mode, sawtooth accumulator, 6-bit resistor-ladder output, the Famicom cartridge audio loop (pin 45 out from the 2A03, pin 46 back to RF) and its absence on the NES; 16K+8K PRG and eight 1K CHR banks, the VRC IRQ, VRC6a/VRC6b address-line swap (iNES 24 and 26); the three games (Akumajō Densetsu, Mōryō Senki MADARA, Esper Dream 2); NSF/FamiTracker and Shovel Knight; Hidenori Maezawa's attributed design account. Coverage checked: no entry, title, alias or redirect; hardware/vrc2 never discusses it; passing mentions in apu, cartridge, NES, mmc5, castlevania, shovel-knight, famitracker and famicom-disk-system. Open and closed website issues and PRs searched; no writing issue or draft. introduced 1989 (22 December 1989, two sources); discontinued left unset. Disagreement recorded: Famitsu.com (2015) names MADARA as the first VRC6 game, against Maezawa (2009), GAME Watch (2023) and NESdev's release list. Source leads: Kevin Horton, VRCVI Chip Info (1999); Firebug's mapper document v0.80; NESdev wiki VRC6, VRC6 audio, VRC6 pinout, Cartridge connector and NSF pages; Maezawa's 1UP.com interview (2009); Retro Gamer 119; GAME Watch and Famitsu.com (Japanese). No period magazine coverage found; Konami's own VRC6 document is not publicly available. Gaps: checkable release dates for MADARA and Esper Dream 2. Draft and claim check done; follow-ups VC-3199 to VC-3204.
